messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night that changed Amir’s life began like any other shift in Mosul, a cramped makeshift clinic in the ruins of an abandoned school. He was a relief worker, a young man from Mumbai who had come to the war zone hoping to give his dance skills a new purpose: moving patients with gentle, rhythmic motion to ease the trauma that clung to their bodies. On the third day, a sudden explosion ripped through the building; a wall collapsed, sending shards of plaster and shattered glass into the air. Amir’s partner was hit, the sound of her scream echoing off the stone walls. He was the first to dive into the chaos, grabbing her, pulling her out as debris fell around them. The heat of the burning fuel that had caught from the damaged electrical lines filled the air, and in that instant his world narrowed to the smell of burning plastic, the taste of blood, and the weight of that single, desperate breath he took to keep moving. For weeks afterward, the memory of that day sat in Amir’s mind like a stone in his chest, a relentless echo that refused to fade. At exactly 3:15 p.m.—the time he had finished the rescue and the last patient’s recovery—his mind would unbidden launch into the scene of the collapse, his body tightening as if the wall were about to rise again. He would be sitting at his rehearsal studio, watching his own reflection in the mirror, when the faint scent of alcohol from a bottle left open on the counter would suddenly flood the room, pulling the memory back into the present. The burnt smell from the burnt plastic in the kitchen would do the same, as if the war had leapt out of the rubble and into his apartment. These triggers did more than just flash the event to the surface; they activated every thread of shame and self‑doubt that had woven itself around the trauma. Amir’s sense of self‑efficacy had always been tied to movement: in dance, he found a language that felt true to his values—respect for the body, for rhythm, for the way music could heal. The night of the collapse, he felt he had failed those values. He had moved so quickly to save his partner that he had left another patient unattended; he had thought himself a hero, but the memory now felt like a failure. He began to believe that the very thing that defined him—his disciplined, graceful dance—had been corrupted by the violence he had witnessed. He saw himself as a “bad coper,” his reactions now irrational and unplanned, and he was certain he could not rely on his own body to keep him safe. The shame that flooded his mind each time a trigger surfaced made him withdraw. He would cancel performances in the evenings, refusing to step onto the stage even when the lights dimmed and the music swelled. He avoided the bar at the corner where his friends laughed, fearing that the scent of alcohol would carry the trauma back to him. He no longer rehearsed after dusk; instead, he sat alone in his studio, staring at the empty floorboards that seemed to hum with the memory of shrapnel. In his marriage, these avoidances translated into silent hours. He left the kitchen for the office, leaving his wife to manage the household while he stared at the blank wall. The more he avoided, the more the memory deepened, and the more he felt his values violated. The loop tightened: triggers led to reliving, reliving produced shame, shame amplified his negative appraisals, and those appraisals heightened his sensitivity to future triggers. Amir’s sense of identity, once anchored in the fluidity of dance, began to feel brittle. He began to imagine that every time he moved—whether to lift a patient or to lift a partner—he risked exposing the fissures of his trauma. The fear of being judged, of failing again, made him increasingly self‑critical. He would catch himself looking at his own hands and thinking, “I am not the dancer I used to be; I am just a man who cannot protect.” That self‑critical thought, a negative appraisal, would then make the scent of burnt plastic or the smell of alcohol even more terrifying, because he imagined that any small cue could trigger the same nightmare. Over months, the cycle became a silent, relentless rhythm. By the time Amir finally walked into a therapist’s office, his days were punctuated by avoidance, his nights filled with reliving the collapse at 3:15 p.m., and his mind flooded with shame whenever a smell reminded him of burning. He was 41, still married, but the partnership had been strained by the growing distance he kept between himself and the people who loved him. He had stopped dancing at the studio he once considered a sanctuary, and he felt his body becoming an instrument of fear rather than a vehicle of expression. The last push that brought Amir to seek help was a quiet evening at home when his wife asked him to share what had been bothering him for months. He could not find the words to explain the invisible walls he had built. He was terrified that if he continued to live in this state, he would lose not only his sense of self but also his marriage and his career as a dancer. He was hoping that by confronting the triggers and the shameful memories, he could find a way to dance again—without the fear that his movements might unleash the past. He was afraid of being unable to rise again, but he also clung to the hope that he could reclaim the grace he had once known.
